content.text: Open-loop stability cannot establish closed-loop safety. Continuous-time linear systems are stable when the relevant closed-loop poles have negative real parts, under usual finite-dimensional LTI assumptions. A nonlinear local linearization can be useful near an operating point, but a plant may have multiple equilibria, regions of attraction, actuator limits and physical states that cannot be expressed by the linear model. Lyapunov-function methods can certify specific regions if assumptions and derivative conditions are established; the existence of a simulation trace with bounded states is not itself a Lyapunov proof. content.text: Continuous-time dynamics and sampled dynamics require an explicit hold convention. For piecewise constant inputs held over a sample period Δ, the exact discrete update is `y[k+1]=a y[k]+b u[k]`, with `a=exp(−Δ/τ)` and `b=K(1−a)`. This zero-order-hold conversion follows by integrating the first-order differential equation. It is not the same as Euler approximation `a≈1−Δ/τ`, which can produce misleading behavior at large Δ. MathWorks documents the ZOH convention for conversion of continuous LTI models to sampled systems. A real digital controller also has conversion, sampling jitter, computational latency, quantization, scheduling and delay; none are present in the toy update. content.text: Integral action can wind up when actuator command exceeds physical limits. MathWorks presents two documented anti-windup approaches—back-calculation and clamping—on a first-order process with actuator saturation and dead time. This Atlas implements only a **specific, discrete conditional integration** convention in a synthetic first-order, no-delay plant: `u=clip(kp*(r−y)+I, umin, umax)`. It freezes I when the proposed command is beyond a rail and the error would push it farther out; otherwise it integrates `I += ki Δt (r−y)`. The state update occurs after actuation via a zero-order-hold discrete model. The `none` mode integrates regardless of saturation. Domain context: 07_pi_pid_saturation_and_anti_windup.md. Near-singular matrices are numerically delicate, and absolute determinant tolerance changes under state scaling: this tool is a teaching calculation, not a condition-number-aware diagnostic for a calibrated system. content.text: A failed sufficient small-gain check does not prove real instability. The small-gain theorem offers a useful **sufficient** stability condition for the feedback interconnection of suitably stable operators: if compatible induced-gain bounds satisfy `||G||·||Δ||<1`, the appropriate feedback system is stable under its assumptions. The simple helper multiplies two supplied nonnegative bounds; it does not estimate induced norms or verify that the interconnection matches the theorem. If the product is ≥1, this particular sufficient test fails, but that **does not prove** the actual system unstable. Domain context: 11_robustness_margins_and_small_gain.md. content.text: Exact model discretization does not identify the actual plant. For piecewise constant inputs held over a sample period Δ, the exact discrete update is `y[k+1]=a y[k]+b u[k]`, with `a=exp(−Δ/τ)` and `b=K(1−a)`. This zero-order-hold conversion follows by integrating the first-order differential equation. It is not the same as Euler approximation `a≈1−Δ/τ`, which can produce misleading behavior at large Δ. MathWorks documents the ZOH convention for conversion of continuous LTI models to sampled systems. A real digital controller also has conversion, sampling jitter, computational latency, quantization, scheduling and delay; none are present in the toy update.
